Uniform Title: Kulālaśāstra Manuscript: IFP/EFEO Transcript T0452 Description: This is a tantra revealed through a certain [deity].
The Kulāla-ṛṣi, the Potter Sage. This work contains a series of ritual procedures (*vidhi*) commonly required in the course of ritual performance,
such as the consecration of the sacrificial jar (*kalaśa*) and other sacred objects.
[The text covers] consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), purificatory rites (*śaucya*), and so forth. The principal deity is the Teacher (*śāstṛ*), namely Skanda.

The treatise on the potter’s craft, the ritual sprinkling, and the eighteen purificatory rites.
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, has four arms, and possesses a serene countenance.
To the elephant-faced one, served by hosts of spirits, who eats the essence of the kapittha and jambu fruits,
the son of Umā, the cause of the destruction of sorrow.
I bow to the lotus feet of Vighneśvara.

During the northern course of the sun, in an auspicious month, under the asterisms of Uttara, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Uttarabhādrapadā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Maghā, Hasta, Citrā, Abhijit, Svātī, Anurādhā, and Revatī; on the second, third, fifth, seventh, or eleventh lunar day;
and during the Amṛta-yoga, Siddhi-yoga, Śubha-yoga, and Śuddha-yoga.
The sin of the king, the sin of the domestic priest, the loss of the patron, the destruction of wealth and grain, the destruction of health, a year devoid of rain, and the consecration— p. 2).
Installation, consecration by sprinkling, and Hari—Om!
This is the eighteenfold sacrament.
The four purificatory rites (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*) are inspection, sprinkling, striking, and pouring over.
The eighteen purificatory rites (*aṣṭādaśa-saṃskāra*) are digging, scattering [soil], filling, leveling, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, and smearing.

Having performed the eighteen purificatory rites— namely, the conceptualization of the constituent parts (*kalāmaya-kalpanā*), the winding with the three threads (*trisūtra-veṣṭana*), the drawing of lines (*rekhā-catur-vinyāsa*), the transformation into a vajra (*vajrīkaraṇa*), the conceptualization of the four feet (*catuṣpāda-kalpanā*), and the supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*)— one should first [establish] the sequence of fire, moon, and nectar for the gods, O Pulastya.
One should place Tāra in the south, and likewise Bhṛgu in the southwest.
Mārkaṇḍeya [is the son] of Varuṇa, and Vasiṣṭha [is the son] of Vāyu in due order; having made Kauśika [the son] of Soma, [he likewise made] Agastya [the son] of Īśa.
Hariḥ oṃ.
May there be auspiciousness.
The Treatise on the Potter.
The introduction to the Tantra.
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who is clothed in white garments, moon-colored, four-armed, and possesses a serene countenance.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various jewels,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and beautified by manifold flowers.
There, in the center, sat the God of gods, Maheśvara, comfortably seated together with various hosts of Gaṇas and the assemblies of Rudra deities.
Having bowed their heads to the ground, Brahmā addressed these words to the sages of great purity, along with the hosts of Gandharvas and others.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to that Lord of the gods, to Śiva, the Supreme Self;
to Rudra, the God of gods, to Śaṅkara, the Self-born.
Salutations to Him whose limbs are pure with ashes, who bestows benefit upon those learned in the four Vedas,
who is the source of the four-faced Brahmā’s manifestation, and who is the heart of the four ears.
To the one who exists as the present for the sake of the future, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
to the one worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and the gods, and the refuge of all the worlds.
Salutation to Time, to the one whose form is Time, and to the end-maker of even the Destroyer of Time;
to the one who pierces through the manifold illusions of the universe, to the All-pervading One, and to the one whose form is the universe.
Salutation indeed to the blue-throated one, to the all-encompassing, to Sadyojāta;
salutation indeed to Vāmadeva, whose form is that of Viṣṇu.
Salutations again and again to Mahādeva, to Haṃsa, to Aghora; salutations again and again to Bhava, to Udbhava, to Śānta, and to Tatpuruṣa.
Salutations again and again to the divine Lord Umānātha,
to Īśāna, to Sadāśiva, the peaceful one, the creator of the universe who is both being and non-being.
Salutations again and again to the sky, whose form is the void, who pervades the sky;
salutations to you, the infinite, salutations again and again to bliss.
"Tell me, O Lord of the gods, the supreme majesty of the scripture.
Īśvara said:
"Excellent, excellent! [It is] for the sake of the virtuous and brings benefit to all the worlds."
For the sake of accomplishing all desired objects and for the destruction of all diseases.
It is the supreme bringer of all accomplishments, the highest remover of all sins,
and the cause of the division between the gods and the asuras through the eating of the honey.
Assuming a form that enchants, Viṣṇu’s delicate and most beautiful consort deceived the asuras and gave the food to the gods.
But having seen Śiva, the supreme cause, the teacher, and the creator of all, Mohinī, out of delusion, spoke those words to him.
The Puruṣa is Hara, and Śakti is Hara; from the union of these two, that [world] comes into being.
It is like fragrance in a flower, and likewise like the vital breath (prāṇa) in the body.
And just as oil exists within sesame seeds, O dear ones, so does your origin exist.
Mādhava is declared to be Prakṛti, and Śiva likewise is Puruṣa;
from the union of Śiva and Mādhava, the Great Wonder, Brahman, is said to arise.
The Teacher is the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation for all things, both moving and unmoving;
he is the Teacher and the descent of the scriptures—therefore, he has been served by you.
I shall speak for the sake of protecting all; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
There are four kinds of Tantras and four kinds of listeners.
Umā, Hari, Skanda, Dhātṛ, Śrotṛ,
and Śrotā [constitute] the Pārvatītantra, which is called the Peaceful (Śāntika) by name.
The *Śrotā* is for Nārāyaṇa, the *Raktā* for the Vijaya[-tantra],
and the *Raudra* is prescribed as the *Adhivra-tantra* of Skanda.
And the Tantra was given to Śrīkaraṇṭāya, whose grandfather was Srotas;
it consists of eighty-one chapters of the Tantras, each distinct from the others.
The individual enumerations of the tantras are declared to be six thousand;
the total collection of tantras consists of twenty-four thousand.
Thus, the fourfold tantra is here spoken of as being accessible through the scriptures;
likewise, listen to the various tantras according to the path taught in this tantra.
May Śiva grant it to the Goddess; may the Goddess grant it to Nandin;
may it have been granted to Nandin by Brahmā, and to Brahmā by the sages.
(6) "Given to the sages by humans"— from these [words], it arises from scripture (āgama).
That which is declared as arising from scripture should be performed in this very manner in its entirety.
The scripture (śāstra) and tradition (āgama) are here spoken of by means of the fourfold mantra;
and the scripture and tradition are [established] through the mantra, together with the collection (saṃhitā), according to the sequence of the limbs (sāṅgata).
One who knows the Āraṇa-sūtra and the Vāṭa, as well as the Ācārya,
the Vyāhṛtis, the Mantras, the Sāvitrī, and the Havyavāhana-mantra.
Recite the *Kṛṇuṣva* mantra with the *Vāja*, as well as the *Prasugmantā*;
likewise, have the reciter chant the *Śrī Rudra*, the *Puruṣa Sūkta*, and the *Camaka*.
By means of this mantra-ritual, those devoted to this scripture [attain their goal];
likewise, those devoted to all mantras as well as to all scriptures [attain theirs].
Having thus performed the recitation of the mantra, listen likewise to that which arises from the Tantra;
it shall be the counsel for yogins, ascetics, and sages.
This worship is prescribed according to the method taught in the Tantra;
likewise, [the worship] of the son of Brahmā, Ambhas, and Ambhasas, as well as Putrada and Antaka.
Dāntaputra was Jaṭādhārī; his son was Kulālaka.
Yāgasva was the sage, and Kulālaka was the maker of clay [objects]; these are the Kulālakas.
O Indra, having come here and performed a sacrifice, he was named Muni;
because he is preeminent by lineage, he is called Kulāla for that reason.
The Brahmans are the vessel for the ritual action, while the potter is merely the maker of the clay;
the sequence of the potter’s procedure consists entirely in the abandonment of the jar to all the gods.
(7) Among the four castes, even among sages, the potter is indeed a brahminical seer (*brāhma-ṛṣi*).
O best of sages, the potter is one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas.
One should perform the initiation of the Teacher, which is endowed with the sacrifice of Tantra and Mantra;
and one should always wear the topknot and the sacred thread, O Prajāpati.
Intent upon libations, recitation, fire-offerings, and the performance of the twilight rituals,
[he studied] the scriptures concerning the rites of worship according to the essential manuals of the various lineages, both ancient and recent.
Performing recitation at the three junctions of the day, wearing the topknot and the sacred thread,
one should have all vessels fashioned for the sake of the gods and for the sake of the Brahmins.
Devotion to the Divine excels a thousand performers of Soma sacrifices;
a potter excels a thousand devotees of the Divine.
The wise man who honors the Teacher with even a single handful of water is better than a potter who honors him with thousands;
this manual of Dharma bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.

This scripture is remembered as the Teacher [itself], encompassing everything from the initial plowing to the consecration, from the consecration to the festival, and from the festival to the final propitiatory rite.
His worship was indeed worthy of praise, and everything he undertook was characterized by restraint;
likewise, his conduct and behavior were refined according to the forty [virtues].
For the purpose of bathing the gods and so forth, for the sacrificial rites of the twice-born,
for the consecration of kings, and indeed for the attainment of perfection by Brahmā;
The characteristics of all vessels and the characteristics of the sacrificial vessel are declared to be the "Kulāla-śāstra," which brings benefit to all living beings.
Thus, the *strīkara-tantra* shall be threefold in its divisions; likewise,
there is the threefold division of the *saṃhitā*, the *dhyāna*, and the *kalpa*.
The rites beginning with plowing and ending with consecration (pratiṣṭhā) are called the *saṃhitā*;
thereafter follows the chapter on the worship mantra, which bestows the boons of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having performed the desired rites, he should follow the procedure prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa-kalpa;
having performed that according to the method of the Saṃhitā-dāna, he fulfilled the desire of his family.
One should worship for one's own sake in due order according to the procedure taught in this chapter;
furthermore, it serves to accomplish various desired objects and to destroy thieves and enemies.
For those who recite mantras, the ritual action must be performed according to the path taught in the scriptures;
this ritual procedure of the tantra is called the yoga of the potter.
The path of the *saṃhitā* is also declared to be suitable for others;
O Grandfather, I shall here describe all these ritual acts.
Thus ends the first chapter, named the Śrīkara Tantra, within the Kaulāla Śāstra, a scripture proclaimed by Īśvara. || 1 ||
Now, I shall duly explain the characteristics of the *tantus* (threads) in their proper order:
beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) and ending with *vivāha* (marriage), as well as up to the sixteenth [rite].
The procedure for the fire-ritual has been declared; now hear the characteristics of the threads.
Brahmā said:
Whether she be a Brāhmaṇī, a princess, a daughter of a Vaiśya,
or even a daughter of a Śūdra, she should prepare the threads.
Having likewise taken cotton, one should prepare the threads;
at the morning time, first [one should perform] the Sāvitrī and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
A cord measuring ninety-six [units] with a width of four finger-breadths is declared to be the long cord, which is three times that [width] in thickness.
The right hand should be raised upward with the tip pointing eastward, while the other [hand] is held behind by the householder;
for the student (brahmacārī), there should be three threads, whereas for the householder, it should be double.
The third stage is that of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the fourth should be that of the renunciant (saṃnyāsin).
[If the breath] goes above the navel, it shortens one's lifespan; if below the navel, it results in the loss of wealth.
One should make the sacred thread (upavīta) reaching to the navel;
the syllable Om is its first strand, and the second is the deity Agni.
The third has Nāga as its presiding deity; the fourth has Soma as its presiding deity;
the fifth has Vāyu as its presiding deity; and the sixth has the Pitṛs as its presiding deity.
The seventh has the Sun as its deity, the eighth has Viṣṇu as its deity, and the ninth has Rudra as its deity; these are the deities of the threads.
Through the three qualities (guṇas), there arises the triad of forms; Śiva is the supreme power of bondage.
By means of the thread-bearer, the Brāhmaṇa [attains] that Śiva who is to be known according to the prescribed rule.
I shall describe the procedure for those who wear matted hair, as well as the sequence of rites for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas;
the procedure for the Vairavānasa has been declared, and the potter wears the sacred thread.

I shall describe the procedure for wearing matted hair, as well as the sequence of rules for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; for a Vaiśya, O best of Śaivas, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) consists of three strands.
These indeed are the characteristics of the ten stages of renunciation;
by maintaining these stages, one should always follow the prescribed sequence.
For the sake of the gods and for the sake of the brahmins, the wearing of the sacred thread should be threefold;
if a śūdra wears the thread, the king and his kingdom perish.
"The village and the village chief, as well as the earth and so forth, one should reduce to ashes by means of *ehi*.
Thus ends the description of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) in the *Kulāla-śāstra* proclaimed by Brahmā.
Having performed the worship of all the gods according to the ritual sequence for all the worlds,
he should likewise establish the procedure for the worship of Brahmā and for the Brāhmaṇas.
Having performed the ritual for the worship of Viṣṇu according to the Vaikhānasa Pāñcarātra,
and having performed the ritual for the worship of Śiva, one is designated as a Śivadvija.
Having performed the worship of the Noble Teacher, as well as the potter and the Brahman-sage,
one should worship the Buddha, Māra, and Pañca according to the ritual sequence.
O Bhadrakālī, perform the worship according to the Śaiva ritual procedure;
for each of these deities, worship them in such a way that each respective god is pleased.
If one fails to worship those respective deities, the kingdom and the realm will perish;
there will be a year of famine, as well as strife and the destruction of the royal administration.
Having performed each of those prescribed rites of worship for a full year, the king thus attained the merit of progeny as a sacrificer.
One should establish the installation of a deity in both a village and a city— a city filled with people that increases longevity and health.
In the center is the abode of the Vāstu-devas; in the east, the Teacher (Śāstṛ) is established;
the place of Agni and Vighneśvara is in the south; and Brahmā is established in the southeast.
In the southwest is the goddess Durgā; in the west, Viṣṇusaṃbhavā;
in the northwest, Mohinī; and in the north, Cāmuṇḍī—such is the sequence.
Having established Hari in the middle direction, these are the deities in their sequence;
having performed the ritual for the placement of the deities, the ritual for the human [officiant] is now described.
The Ālaya is the site for a householder; likewise, the Brāhmaṇa is in the south, the Nagara in the west, and the Rājadhānika in the north.
To the south and to the north, the royal station (rājasthāna) is prescribed;
and to the east, in the region of the Śūdras—thus it should be arranged in sequence in the four directions.
Whether in a village or a city, the site-plan (vāstu) of potters is established;
from the site-plan comes the creation of the planets—these [rites] bestow purity upon the house.

The rules for entering the houses of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, as well as the entry into the dwellings of those of the lowest castes (antyajātis), which are fraught with defects, have been explained. One should avoid the latter; however, the ritual for a festival of the gods and the sacred ground of Brahman (brahmadeśa) are purifying.
The region of Brahmā is the most excellent, while that of the city is middling.
The lowest [caste], the Śūdra, [should perform] the procedure for the festival in the region;
the rite for the service of the Teacher’s festival is also [prescribed] in the house of those of low birth.
The other caste, however, produces mantras that lead to excessive faults;
the Kṣatriya, moreover, is of an empty nature, giving rise to all kinds of diseases.
That and that scripture must be composed, which is exceedingly faultless and dear to Mahāripu;
likewise, the Teacher, who wears matted locks and belongs to the potter caste, shall perform the eternal festival.
The noble Teacher has arisen as the single form of Śiva and Śakti;
Mohinī is the form of Viṣṇu, born from the vision of Śiva.
Deluded by the sight of forms, wandering about in the embrace [of passion],
the world— both stationary and moving— is filled with the great terror of blazing fire.
The Lord of the world and the seven realms, the Noble Teacher, was born from that;
from the navel of Viṣṇu was born the son of Īśa, possessed of great strength.
O Lord of all worlds, O Master of the universe, O Noble Teacher, [explain] the origin of that [teaching],
O God of gods, O Lord of the universe, and the sequential procedure for the worship of the potter.
The maker of vessels and the potter perform the horse sacrifice;
by the grace of all the gods, their wealth shall increase.
O all you gods, by your grace, let the potter who worships the Teacher perform [the rites] from the plowing up to the consecration,
and from the consecration up to the festival.
The Teacher [taught] the sequence of ritual procedures from the festivals up to the conclusion of the propitiatory rites;
the Teacher [taught] the specific details of the scriptures, and the Lord [spoke] these supreme words.
In the east, let Agni worship the teacher named Māri;
in the south, let him worship the black-formed Senāpati in the southwest (nair-ṛta).
In the west is Bhūtanātha, and in the northwest is Eka-vīthika;
in the north is Dhīnu-bhera, and in the northeast is the Liṅga of the Teacher.
In both the village and the city, to the north of the royal precinct,
one should worship the Teacher in his eightfold form (Aṣṭamūrti) and first in his form of enjoyment (Bhogamūrti).
In the southeast corner is the full form, the Saṃhāra-nṛtta image;
in the west is the painted image, and in the northwest is the Yoga image.
In the north is the bed-image, and in the northeast is the image of Śāstṛ;
there are eight images of Śāstṛ, and the Kṣatriya [image] is eight *kalās* in size.
At the time of the king's birth, the form of the deity was painted on a cloth;
at the time of the commencement of his letters, the painted image was consecrated.
At the time of the weapons [consecration], the Dancing Form (nṛttabera) is installed;
and at the time of the consecration, the Enjoyment Form (bhogamūrti) is installed.
At the time when the son was born, the Liṅga-form was installed;
and at the time of Dharmakoṭīra, the Yoga-form was installed.
Having established the image for the period of sleep at the conclusion of the time of full knowledge,
and having performed the ritual for all the deities— such are the rites for a Kṣatriya.
In the east, the two-armed Bhogaberanta is prescribed by the rule;
in the southeast is Saṃhāra with sixteen hands;
and in the south is Vīramūrti with eight hands, according to the sequence of the rule.
In the southwest, there should be a painted cloth [image] measuring ten cubits; or alternatively,
in the west, a painted image in relief with four arms, measuring one cubit.
In the northwest, the Yoga image should be twelve cubits;
in the north, the Śayana image is prescribed by the rule as having six arms.
In the northeast is Dhanuṣe-ra, and the twelfth is Hastameva;
the names of the elephants are Ārya and Śāsta, and the mount is the horse.
In the south is Kṛṣṇamūrti, whose vehicle is indeed a dog;
and Nairṛta is the commander of the army, whose vehicle is a cock.
In the west, Bhūtanātha, who has a ram as his vehicle;
and in the northwest, Yogabera, who likewise has a tiger as his vehicle.
In the north is the image of Śayana, whose vehicle is a lion;
and in the northeast is the image of Dhanu, whose vehicle is a bull.
The procedure for the lotus posture (padmāsana) as proclaimed by the rules, the sequence of rites for the form of the Liṅga,
and the syllable 'Go'.
Cow's ghee should be from a tawny cow, curd is said to be from a white cow,
the milk should be yellow-colored, and the cow dung red-colored.
A wise person should collect black-colored cow urine;
ghee should be prepared with one *prastha*, and two *prasthas* of curd are prescribed.
A wise person should collect three prasthas of milk, four prasthas of cow dung,
and five prasthas of cow urine.
15) The Characteristics of the Teacher:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the teacher.
The teacher shall possess purity of strength and be devoted to truth and righteousness.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, proficient in all scriptures,
possessed of every skillful means, truthful in speech, and firm in his vows.
Having endowed him with the initiation of the scriptures and making him a protector of the conduct of the observances,
one should fashion the form of the mantra within the thirty-two characteristics.
The limb of yoga for Tantric practice is the mantra associated with union (sāyujya),
together with the topknot and the sacred thread, which maintains the conduct of the observances.
Endowed with knowledge of the grammatical cases, he is not clever at worldly affairs; he should be free from delusion and dejection, and devoid of desire and anger.
The power of mantra is pure power; it is the wise one who is devoted to the dharma of truth, whose mind is free from torment, and devoid of conceptual construction.
Engaged in recitation and meditation, free from partiality,
patient, devoid of leprosy, and rid of chronic diseases.
He has no eye disease, nor is he lame, nor is he water-born, nor likewise is he one-eyed; furthermore, he does not have protruding teeth, nor is he overly tall, nor is he a dwarf.
One who is not too corpulent, who is ungrateful, who has avoided base pursuits,
and who lacks the capacity for violence in his eyes and ears— such a person one should avoid.

One who lacks fingers or hands, or is deprived of the corners of the feet; yet who is devoted to the Guru, the deities, and others, and who possesses the virtues of austerity and affection for good qualities.
For one who is sinless yet heedless, though capable, is not a detractor;
he is a destroyer of obstacles, a knower of the authoritative means, and a triple-knower through the form of the mantra.
One who knows the treasury of all treatises and is devoted to all mantras—
endowed with such characteristics, he is called a master potter.
The characteristics of the teacher have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the disciples.
First is the invocation, and second is the installation.
One should offer the third [offering] with water for the feet, the fourth as water for sipping (ācamanīyaka),
the fifth as the placement of the respectful offering (arghya), and the sixth should be the ceremonial bath (abhiṣecana).
The seventh is clothing and incense; the eighth is the worship with flowers;
the ninth should be incense and lamps; and the tenth is the food offering.
One should perform the eleventh offering (bali) during the twelfth rite of fire-oblation (homa);
one should perform the thirteenth offering, and the fourteenth consists of song and instrumental music.
The fifteenth is indeed dance, and the sixteenth is marriage;
with these sixteen services, there shall be the accomplishment of all desired aims.
The invocation was previously described, as well as the installation and the water-offering (arghya);
likewise, the perfume, flower, incense, lamp, and food offering.
The dismissal and the sipping of water (ācamana) are proclaimed as the ten modes of service (daśopacāra).
The procedure for purification (p. 17).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual of purification;
one should perform it while reciting the hundred-fold mantra over the morning and evening oblations.

Having risen early in the morning and performed ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should avoid villages and the like for a distance of a hundred *daṇḍas*, as well as temples, cow-pens, trees, and places frequented by birds.
One should avoid [wearing] the sacred thread above the ear on a riverbank, by a pond, or at any holy site;
rather, it should be worn at the ear or at the root of the ear.
Having spread grass in a clean place toward the south of the sun,
or alternatively toward the west, the potters should stand there.
One should likewise perform the cleansing of the mind and the breath;
having grasped the penis with the left hand, one should take up earth with the right.
Having cleansed them at a pond on the riverbank,
the potter should take these vessels and water, and then perform the purification.
Having specifically measured ten portions with the palm of the hand as the measure,
one should purify both hands with clay using three portions for the penis.
Thus has purity been described; now listen likewise to the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for ācamana in its proper sequence.
One should wash them as with the feet, likewise placing the left foot in the water;
then, having done so for the other foot, one should insert the hands [into the water].
Having drunk water with the hand [cupped] to the size of a cow’s ear, there shall be a threefold [act].
Afterwards, one should press the thumb; listen now to the procedure for *ācamana* as well.
Having spread out one's hands, one should first touch the thumbs;
then, joined with the ring fingers, they should come into contact with the eyes.
The joining of the thumb and forefinger should be applied to the two nostrils;
the joining of the little finger and thumb should be applied to the two ears.
One should join the middle finger with the thumb and place both arms [in that position];
having placed the thumb at the navel, one should place the four fingers at the heart.
Likewise, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with all the fingers at the head;
and having performed the bath in water reaching only up to the navel, O potters.
Having performed the placement of the Brahmāṅga, one should place it in the midst of the water;
having cast the Śāstṛ-mantra into the water, the Śāstṛ should then prepare the sacred bathing site (tīrtha).
A small amount of head-ointment, rubbing the limbs, and anointing with turmeric; likewise, massaging the thumb brings auspiciousness.
Having bathed again at the ford of the Teacher, one should likewise perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again;
then, during the time of dawn, [one should recite] the mantra beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ."
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the Sūrya-mantra, one should sprinkle [the offerings] with the Dadhi-mantra.
Having placed the Goddess Sāvitrī [in her seat], one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with the Sāvitrī-mantra.
At the taking up of the nine [vessels] and the satiation, one should perform the Sāvitrī, the sipping of water (ācamana), and the ten [recitations];
at the worship with the *āyātu* mantra, one should again mutter the Sāvitrī.
Having performed one hundred and eight prostrations with the Indra-mantra,
and having performed the midday sipping of water (ācamana), the knower of mantras should recite the "Āpaḥ punantu" mantra.
Having performed the libations for others as before,
one should especially perform the libation for the deities and likewise the libation for the sages (ṛṣis).
Having performed the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa), one should practice the subsidiary rite of the Brahma-sacrifice (brahmayajña);
specifically, one should recite the Sāvitrī mantra twenty-eight times once again.
Having approached for the ritual attendance with mantras, as previously described for others,
one should likewise perform the recitation of mantras upon approaching at evening time.
The attendance [of the deity] is performed specifically with this Vāruṇa mantra;
for others, one should proceed as before with the recitations of the potter and the noble ones.
Or else, one should recite it one hundred and eight times again, both at dawn and at dusk;
at dawn one should recite the mantra while standing, and at dusk while seated.
Having circumambulated these [images] clockwise, one should offer salutations to the suns;
likewise, one should perform prostrations in the four directions and toward oneself as the preceptor.
Having offered salutations in the seven directions with their respective mantras in particular,
and having thus propitiated Sāvitrī, one should fix the mind single-pointedly.

The knower of mantras, consisting of fivefold self, should sprinkle the fire— the fire of the sacrificial fuel as well as the fire of the mantra— with the *caṇḍavaktra* and other mantras, beginning with the utterance of *svāhā*.
One should perform the ritual salutation with the mantra beginning "yatte agne" while reciting it in sequence;
having discarded the wet garment, one should wrap oneself in a clean, auspicious cloth.
Having approached the Teacher with the mantra, one should perform three circumambulations in succession;
then, having performed the eightfold and fivefold placement, one should offer the prostration in the *daṇḍaka* style.
The performance of the twilight rites has been declared; now hear that which is called the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Thus, the procedure for the placement on the limbs is completed.
The characteristics of the water-pot.
For women, the *prapautara* [vessel] is prescribed, but not the *puṃsavana* or the jars;
it is said that the depth should be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) less than the height, while the width at the base should be two finger-breadths.
The lips, fingers, sleep, the anus, the genitals, and the exit;
there, O Vāyu, you have ripened these fruits for them.
Having the shape of a ripe bimba fruit, devoid of a black spot,
and filled with thirty-two prasthas— these are the characteristics of a ritual jar (kumbha).
The wise man [perceives] the jewel, the tendon, the flesh, and the earth itself;
yet the deities are to be measured by water, blood, and earth.
The *kūrca* should be joined to the tongue; one should wrap the hide with a cloth.
The coconut is for the head, the eye is the coconut, and the hairy [leaf] is the mango sprout.
The seven elements are likewise present in the jars and pots;
at the mouth of the large water-pot (kumbha) is Rudra, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity in its center.
At the base, the deities are Brahmā and the others; in the belly are Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī;
on the two sides are Brahmā and Viṣṇu; and for these, the presiding deities are the jars (kumbhas).
One should worship the water situated within the pitcher, the lotus within the water,
and within that lotus, the Śāstra together with its limbs (aṅgas).
Having placed a jar filled with meat and water, one should place the vital breath (prāṇa) within;
then, having wrapped it with threads, it should be bound with a single thread.
The triple-threaded cord is said to be peaceful; it is made of barley-strands and is not [merely] discarded.
The best is the size of a sesame seed, while the middling is the size of a barley grain.
The characteristic of this [measurement] is the joint of the lowest finger;
its length is eight cubits and its width is two cubits.
One should wrap a white, beautiful pitcher with a hand;
for the *vardhanī* vessel, it is six *hasta*s, and for the *kalaśa*, four *hasta*s.
One should place the five jewels— diamond, emerald, lapis lazuli,
coral, and pearl— into the Śiva-pitcher.
If the cloth is missing, there will be a great disease; if the thread is missing, death;
if the tuft is missing, deformity; and the flower and fragrance will be fruitless.
If the coconut is deficient, the village will likewise become desolate;
if the water containing jewels is deficient, the daily worship perishes.
If the vessel of nectar is deficient, it brings both misfortune and suffering.
22) [Now follows] the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas); listen to that which is beneficial for all the world, meritorious, and intended for the welfare dear to all the gods.
One should consider the seat of Śruti as triangular, that of Yoni as bow-shaped, that of Anya as circular,
that of Bhūta as pentagonal, the Arghya of Paṅkaja as octagonal, and the Koṇaka of Śraddhā as having eight corners.
For ten million oblations (koṭi-homa), the altar should be eight cubits; for one hundred thousand (lakṣa-homa), six cubits; and for a thousand (sahasra-homa), two cubits.
The girdle (mekhalā) should be made of seasonal flowers, with its width increasing by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in each successive case.

In the case of a four-cubit [image], the measurements are eight and four *aṅgulas* respectively for the *kauśika*; in the case of a six-cubit [image], they are known as ten, nine, and eight *aṅgulas*, which is called the "Eight Auspicious Ones" (*aṣṭamaṅgala*).
In the case of an eight-cubit [fire-pit], one should likewise make it ten finger-breadths [in depth] for each of the Sun (twelve) and Rudra (eleven);
whatever the shapes of the fire-pits may be, such shall be the shape of the girdles as well.
The width should be one finger-breadth (anyāṅgula), while the divine measure is five finger-breadths (bhūtāṅgula);
the opening should gradually taper to a thinness like a pipal leaf.
The characteristics of the womb (yoni) have been described; one should fashion it upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Its height is proclaimed to be one-third of its width.
Beginning from two cubits and extending up to eight cubits,
the width should be increased by one *aṅgula* at a time, while the length should be increased by two *aṅgulas*.
The characteristic of the *yoni* should be thus; one should fashion it above the girdle (*mekhalā*), with a height of five finger-breadths and a width of three finger-breadths.
The shape [of the pit] should be like a lotus, extending from the navel to the center of the *kuṇḍa*;
it should have a measurement of two parts for the petals, while the pericarp (*karṇikā*) shall be one part.
Beginning from two cubits and proceeding in order up to eight cubits,
the width increases by one *aṅgula* at each step, and the height increases by half an *aṅgula*.

The characteristic of the navel should not be thus; rather, one should determine its width. And the pit (kuṇḍa) should extend all around to the edge, measuring one cubit (hasta) by means of finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Starting from two cubits and extending up to eight cubits,
one should prepare the sacrificial seat (viṣṭara), increasing it by half a finger-breadth at each step.
One should cause the expansion of the supreme beauty of the womb,
the rim, and the nave to be constructed either with bricks baked by their own heat (*svadhā-pakva*) or with clay.
For the purpose of drawing the circles of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should first construct a square;
then, having laid down the eastern thread, one should mark the "fish" (intersection) in the south and north.
One should mark from west to east according to the width of the pit;
then, having made it square, one should divide it into four compartments.
For all fire-pits (kuṇḍas) as well, the triangle is said to be the womb (yoni);
likewise, by means of a square (vimāna), it is [formed] from half the ear on both sides of half the field (kṣetra).
Having measured out the dimensions of the field, one should deposit [the central point] at the midpoint of the field;
having divided that which is in excess there into two parts, one should proceed clockwise toward the south and north.
The wise man should place each one outside the thread and then inside; by that same measure, he should draw a bow-shaped curve on the ground toward the north.
In the field, however, within the portion belonging to the Bhūtas, one should place a single part on each of the two sides; furthermore,
another [part] should be placed there in the south-west and the north-west directions.
Having made a thread three times one *aṅgula* in length, and having attached it to the tail of the fish by means of a triangle, it is then known as the stretched line for the triangle.
One should take half of the ear and cast half of the field;
having divided the excess there into two parts, one should place the portion of space on the outside.
By means of that same measurement, the circular pit (kuṇḍa) is described;
it is circular with one-sixth part [of the side] or indeed with half of the area.

Then, taking that difference and dividing it by its own part, O serpent, the result multiplied by the part of the element (five) shall be the clear [result]. The end of the elements (five) shall indeed be the precise value.
Then, having divided that field into four parts, one should set aside each single portion;
with half the measurement of that field, the wise man should form a fish-diagram (matsya).
Its measurement is four-petalled and circular in the four directions;
such is the lotus-pool when the sacrificial field is divided into three parts.
Having set aside one part externally,
[one should draw] a square all around by means of a cord measuring half the diagonal, from corner to corner, for the purpose of leveling the two [sides].
In the four directions, one should construct an eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the proper characteristics;
it should be circular, formed by one-seventh of the area or by half of the field.
One should join together one-sixteenth part of the field and half of that same field; by rotating [the cord] according to the measurement, a clearly defined square is produced.

When [the lunar mansion] is deficient in measure, there is a great disease; when it exceeds, there is an increase of enemies. When it is broken, there is drought; when it is cracked, there is the destruction of crops.
If [the vessel] is broken, it leads to disease; if it is split, there will be strife. The ritual procedure for the abode of the fire is either a pit (kuṇḍa) or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
When the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is made square, it accomplishes all desired objectives;
when it is in the shape of a womb (yoni), it increases progeny; and when it is half-moon shaped, it is highly efficacious.
A triangular pit is said to grant peace; a circular one is for the sake of prosperity;
a pentagonal one is for the destruction of disease; and a lotus-shaped one is for the purpose of recitation (japa).
The eight-cornered [pit] is said to bestow nourishment, while the seven-cornered increases crops;
thus has the fruit of the sacrificial pits been declared, and now the altar-ground (sthaṇḍila) is described.
Having smeared the golden niches with cow dung and swept them clean with *darbha* grass,
one should take water in the hollow of the hands, sprinkle it, and worship the two auspicious-faced [deities].
One who [constructs] a pure site that has been sprinkled with water, which is not damp, one *hasta* in width,
three *aṅgulas* in height, and level without depressions or elevations;
There should be three lines with their tips pointing east; likewise, by means of a line with its tip pointing north, one forms an octagon, a square, a heptagon, and a hexagon.
A male [fire-pit] is known as a *kuṇḍa*, or it is called a *kuṇḍa* when it is situated [as a structure];
the fire-pits may be in the shape of a womb (*yoni*), a triangle, a circle, or a lotus.
It is said that the posture of sitting should be made in the form of a woman;
the reclining posture is shaped like a bow and is traditionally known as the neuter.
To the east it should be square; in the southeast, the shape is like a bow;
in the south, a half-moon; and in the southwest, a triangle.
In the west, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is circular; in the northwest, it is hexagonal;
in the north, it is lotus-shaped; and in the northeast, it is octagonal.
"One should cause a circular fire-pit (vṛttakuṇḍa) to be made between the directions of Indra and Īśāna.
Thus ends the procedure for the fire-rite (agnikāryavidhi) in the Kāraṇa [Tantra].
Kuśa, kāśa, uśīra, darbha, bamboo, and likewise barley,
as well as viśvāmitra and mauñjī— these are proclaimed as the eight types of darbha grass.
The interior of the *kuśa* grass is the best; the middle part of the best [grass] would be middling;
the inferior is the *darbha*, and one should likewise avoid thick *darbha* grass.
A wise man should avoid a blade of Darbha grass that is thick at the tip;
he should make the root and the tip equal, for such is the characteristic of a Darbha blade.
One should also avoid a Darbha blade that is deficient at the tip.
One should discard inferior Darbha grass and avoid white Darbha;
the base should be thick, and the tip should likewise be naturally so.
A wise person should perform these rites with a dark complexion;
Rudra is the root of the gods, and Viṣṇu is their source.
"May the foremost [deity] have Brahmā as its presiding deity"— thus is the sequence of deities;
[this concludes] the characteristics of the *pavitra*.
Having performed the two auspicious rites and the single rite for the ancestors,
[one should observe] the characteristics of the kuśa grass, the kuśa-darbha, and the purifiers.
One should increase the length by twice the measure of one cubit;
the tip should be four finger-breadths wide, and there should be one knot of one finger-breadth.
The measurement of the ring for the purifier (pavitra) is two finger-breadths;
its tip has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and likewise, the knot has Viṣṇu.
Īśvara and Valaya—these constitute the sequence of deities;
the worship of the gods, auspicious rites, and the two types of darbha grass that arise therefrom.
The Teacher should bind the ring finger with the root mantra;
such are the characteristics and the measurement of the purifying thread.
One should provide *gopāla*, *kuśa*, and *darbha* grasses, along with purifiers (*pavitra*) joined with gold;
these may be three, five, four, or likewise two, one, or even a single pair.
Just as [the power resides] in the thunderbolt of Rudra, and as it resides in the wielder of the trident;
just as in the discus consisting of Viṣṇu, and as in the purifying thread of Brahmā.
If it occurs on the thumb, there will be disease; on the index finger, death is certain;
on the middle finger, there will be the destruction of sons; and on the little finger, one's actions will be fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, and especially on the ring finger, one should perform the ritual of the *kūrca* according to its defining characteristics.
The tip [of the darbha] should be four finger-breadths long, the knot one finger-breadth,
and the root portion of the darbha should consist of twelve finger-breadths.
At the tip is Īśvara, and likewise Viṣṇu at the knot;
the root has Brahmā as its presiding deity—such is the sequence of the deities.
Seven *darbha* blades for rites of merit (*śubhakarma*) and three for ancestral rites (*pitṛkarma*);
"to you whose form is dark-colored"—such are the characteristics of the *kūrca*.
At the root of the *kūrca* is Pārvatī, likewise at its knot;
and at the tip of the *kūrca* are all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*). Thus is the *kūrca* described.
The two excellent types are the Khadira and the Brahmavr̥kṣa;
the two middling types arise from the Aśvattha and the Udumbara.
The fuel-sticks and apāmārga grass are prescribed for the exorcism;
likewise, one should arrange the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) as follows.
The fuel-stick (*idhma*) consists of sixteen [units], and the production of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) is threefold;
the enclosing stick is one cubit (*hasta*) in measure, and its tip is produced from [the same] source.
The fuel-stick (idhma) should be of this measurement, exactly twelve finger-breadths in length;
its tip has Brahmā as its deity, while the middle part has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
At the base, one should worship Īśvara, and the deities of the enclosing sticks;
likewise for the sixteen-syllable [mantra], and likewise for the sacrificial fuel (idhma) and its deities.
Having thus established these deities, one should then [worship] Brahmā as the source;
one should avoid [an animal] that is devoid of skin here, as well as one that is devoid of tusks.
For children, the characteristic of sacrificial fuel (samidh) is said to be the size of the little finger, excluding the thumb; the same applies to the characteristics of darbha grass.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the worship of the Teacher—
the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa.
[He taught] the Lord of Beings, the Sovereign of the World, the Destroyer of Evil, the Lord of the Universe;
the Teacher, the Manifestation, the Distinction, and the sequential procedure for the worship of the Kulāla.
Having placed a handful of flowers upon the back and the three-eyed [deity] above the feet,
Īśvara said:
"O Lotus-seated One, listen to the classification of images and their worship according to the scriptures."
It indeed bestows longevity and victory, and brings about the attainment of sons and wealth.

The rules for [the construction of] images made of gold, crystal, stone, wood, clay, copper, and lead, as well as those painted or engraved on stone, shall now be explained according to the prescribed ritual.
The painting on cloth, on walls, and so forth shall now be described according to the prescribed rules;
likewise, [the materials] are cloth, wall, stone, gold, clay, and crystal.
Yāgasvāmī was a potter, yet he was a Brahman seer;
by the grace of all the gods, O great teacher, he became a deity.
The ancestors and descendants of the potters, their lineage deities, the Teacher, and those who perform worship—the potters are the most excellent teachers, consecrated by the Teacher. (p. 30)
One should perform worship day after day, which removes all sins;
likewise, they should observe ritual purity, perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana), and circumambulate the temple three times.
One should prostrate on the ground like a staff with the eight limbs and perform obeisance;
there, one should likewise employ the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) for opening the door-panels.
Sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and the ritual characteristics of lamps;
first is the purification of oneself, and second is the purification of the place.
The third is the purification of the substance, and the fourth is the purification of the image;
the fifth is the purification of the mantra, and one should then worship the retinue and other attendants.
Then, beginning with the five purifications, he shall explain the purification of the self;
having positioned himself facing either east or north, he should perform the binding of the directions.
The application of ashes, sandalwood, and flowers to the head, thumbs, and other parts,
followed by placing the Astra-mantra on the palms, is known as the purification of the hands (kara-śuddhi).
Beginning from the head down to the soles of the feet by means of the root mantra,
and from the thumb to the little finger— this is declared to be the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (the rite of emanation).
The wise practitioner, having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), should indeed perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of withdrawal, starting from the feet and heart and ending at the head.
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and the threefold retention (kumbhaka)—
one should perform exhalation there by means of the belly and the nose.
One should likewise avoid both the superior and the inferior types of *kumbhaka*.
Having performed three rounds of *prāṇāyāma*, each consisting of ten *mātrās*.
One should unite the self there at the tip of the crest-lock, twelve finger-breadths [above the head];
the earth extends as far as the knees, and the waters as far as the navel.
The region of the throat is the deity Agni, while the forehead is the deity Vāyu;
one should cause Śiva to reside at the tip of the crest-lock, twelve finger-breadths above.
Likewise, the seed-syllables *la*, *va*, and *ra* are the abodes of the elements and so forth;
they possess five, four, three, two, and one quality respectively.
Then, as if drying it with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, one should burn the triad of qualities and the amātra in the heart; thereafter, [one should visualize] the ash in the form of a cord.
At the tip of the crest-lock, twelve finger-breadths long, the wise one should meditate upon a white lotus facing downwards; there, he should cause nectar to flood it with the moon.

One should fill [the vessel] with nectar and meditate; thus one becomes possessed of a divine body. Having performed the internal sacrifice in this manner, according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the limbs and the ritual placement on the hands;
the wise practitioner should perform the placement beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should assign Vāmadeva to the private parts.
One should place Sadyojāta on the feet; then one should again perform the placement of the limbs (aṅgas):
having placed the heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the head-mantra on the head.
Having assigned the *śikhā* mantra to the crest-lock, the *kavaca* to the middle of the chest, the *netra* to the eyes, and the *astra* to the region of the hands; (p. 32)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight digits (kalās), beginning with the crown (makuṭa) and so forth, in their proper sequence;
then, one should place the Teacher (Śāstā) in the heart by means of the root mantra, following the prescribed order.
Purification by ashes has thus been described; now listen likewise to the purification of the ground.
To the east of the temple door, one should apply a coating of mere ashes.
One should bind the mandala in the eight directions with the Astra-mantra;
there, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of Brahmā, as well as offer flowers and the arghya water within the mandala.
One should likewise worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps the Teacher, his retinue,
the abode of the Prajñās, Agni, and the face of Vighneśvara.
Brahmā is in the southern abode, and the King of Nagas is in the southwest.
The abode of Indra is in the west, the excellent abode in the direction of Vāyu (northwest),
the king Soma in the north, and that of Kṣetrapāla in the northeast.

The Teacher has declared that for those with eight attendants, the auspicious smearing with cow dung is called "purification of the site"; now hear likewise about the "purification of the substances."
One should have the water-vessel, the *vardhanī*, the flower-vessel,
and the *arghya* vessel made from conch-shells or from water-pitchers and other such materials.
One should wash the three-legged stands for the cooking pots, the other vessels such as ladles, and the heart-like central pot; then one should apply an ointment of ash to the *kaṃśā* vessels.
Having filled the *arghya* vessel with water, the Teacher should recite the mantra one hundred times;
the potter should then sprinkle all the vessels with the mantra.
Thus the purification of substances has been declared; now hear from me the purification of mantras.
One should perform every mantra beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should fulfill the mantra there as it is set forth; thus there shall be purity of the mantra.
Having thus explained the purity of the mantra, now hear the worship of the retinue.
First, one should thoroughly worship Airāvata with fragrance and water,
as well as with blue lotuses, jasmine flowers, fragrant blossoms, and incense.
The potter should perform the worship with the mantra for elephants, beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*,
while striking the bell.
One should worship Agni and Vighneśvara, whose vehicle is the mouse;
one should ring the bell, offer incense, water, and perform excellent worship.
One should offer jasmine and *jāti* flowers, as well as white flowers for adornment,
along with the obstacle-removing mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
The potter should strike the bell and perform worship;
on the right, he should worship the lotus-seated Brahmā, whose deity is Brahman.
One should worship the four-faced one, who possesses the four Vedas and is adorned with all ornaments;
likewise, one should offer incense, water, and the striking of the bell.
One should sequentially place the Bhaṭṭamāvaraṇa, as well as the crown and other ornaments;
then flowers such as the lotus, fragrant flowers, incense, and lamps.
Likewise, one should worship with the Brahma-mantra and indeed with that very mantra. One should offer food offerings (naivedya), betel, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and a mirror.
The potter should strike the bell and perform worship;
in the southwest, there is the worship of the Naga, and the [deities] are covered by a cloth with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should draw a square seat and a four-petaled lotus;
one should strike the bell and worship well with fragrance and water.
Having worshipped with blue lotuses, jasmine flowers, turmeric, ointment, yellow cloth, as well as a bell, incense, and a lamp;
One should worship in sequence with honey-milk and then with *bhīṣṭī* as the food offering (*naivedya*),
as well as with betel-leaf, and likewise with the bell, incense, and lamp.
One should worship the Naga kings with the three mantras and indeed with their specific mantra;
in the west, one should worship all the gods, having Indra as their presiding deity.
The blue lotus, the jasmine flower, fragrant flowers, incense, and lamps,
as well as the mantra of the elephants beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
The potter should strike the bell and perform worship;
he should then sequentially place the Bhaṭṭamāvaraṇa, the crown, and so forth.
He has a thousand eyes, four arms, and rides upon an elephant;
in his hands he holds a thunderbolt, a discus, a noose, and a goad.
One should strike the bell, and properly worship with incense,
water, blue lotuses, jasmine flowers, and other white blossoms as ornaments.
Sandalwood, saffron water, and all types of ornaments;
(p. 35) food offerings, betel leaf, as well as the bell, incense, and lamps.
The potter should worship Indra with the mantra beginning "indrādi," and should sequentially present an umbrella, a chowrie, a lamp, and a mirror.
Having thus performed the rites for Indradeva, the potter should worship them;
in the northwest (vāyavya) are Mohinī, Lokavaśyā, and Surākṣasī.
One should especially wrap the lion throne with black-colored cloth and the like;
one should strike the bell and offer incense, water, and excellent worship.
One should worship with a turmeric ointment while reciting that mantra;
having likewise fashioned the Mohinī-bhujaṅga, the potter should perform the worship.
Uttara, Soma, Rāja, Nakṣatra, Svāmī, Suprabha, Śāstārtha, Kāraṇa, Śāstā, and Śāstā-lepana are said here [to be the names of the months].
A thousand kodavas of cloth, the natural form of Śyāmā,
garments such as red garlands, and especially a lion throne.
One should strike the bell, and worship with incense, water, a crown,
a lotus, and flowers adorned with red blossoms.
Having adorned [the deity] with sandalwood, saffron-filled incense, all types of ornaments,
and every kind of jewelry, one should worship with the food offering (naivedya) in due order.
Having likewise worshipped with the Soma-mantra, one should worship the betel-roll well;
then, one should sequentially present the umbrella, the fly-whisk, the lamp, and the mirror.
One should strike the bell and the potter should perform the worship;
in the northeast, one should worship Kṣetrapāla, who is beautiful with all ornaments.
Four-armed, with a dog as his vehicle, beautiful with ornaments of bows,
and likewise beautiful with ornaments of feet including anklets on his feet.
Holding a trident and a skull in her hands, as well as a ḍāmara-drum and a snake-noose,
she is dark-complexioned, draped in [black] garments, and adorned with all ornaments.
One should strike with the bell and offer incense, water, and excellent worship;
having anointed [the deity] with black sandalwood paste, one should adorn it with black flowers.
One should worship with the offering of food (naivedya) and betel leaf using that mantra;
likewise, the potter should ring the bell and perform the worship.
The potter should worship the Teacher together with his eight attendants;
likewise, he should offer the threefold worship consisting of water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya).
Delightful sandalwood is declared to be the substance for the water for the feet (pādya), along with cardamom,
cloves, camphor, and the atimuktaka fruit used for the worship of the directions.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, unbroken rice, barley, grains, sesame seeds, and water with sugar— this is said to be the eightfold arghya offering.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and guggulu—this incense, combined thus, is most excellent; [one should offer it] with the nose and the heart.
The potter should worship white garments and the like, the breaking of the vessel, the rolling of camphor, the eye-mantra, and likewise the lamps.
The sattvic flower is white, the rājasic flower is red,
and the tāmasa flower is black; thus, the flower itself is indeed threefold.
One should place white flowers in the forenoon, red flowers at midday, and black flowers in the afternoon, according to the sequence of the flowers.
One should worship with leaves in the morning, with red flowers at midday,
and with fragrant flowers in the evening, thus worshipping according to the sequence of the three junctions of the day.
In the forenoon, there should be white fragrance; at midday, red sandalwood;
and in the afternoon, all kinds of perfumes; thus the potter should perform the worship.
First is the lion posture (siṃhāsana), second is likewise the elephant posture (gajāsanam), and third is the lotus posture (padmāsana); such is the sequence of these postures.
The lion-posture (siṃhāsana) is prescribed for bathing, the elephant-posture (gajāsanam) for eating, and the lotus-posture (padmāsana) for recreation; such is the sequence of postures.
The sequence beginning with the seat has been declared; now listen likewise to the purification of the image.
One should dismiss the flower worshipped during the morning twilight with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Likewise, there is the dismissal (*visarjana*), flowers adorned with *madhūka*,
bathing facing north, and a beautiful seat for the Teacher.
The potter should strike the bell and perform worship;
he should apply oil and sandalwood paste, as well as an ointment made from his own ground [substance].
The potter should apply [the clay], beginning with the Īśāna direction and ending with the Sadyojāta,
using all the necessary materials, while it is covered by a concealed cloth.
The knower of mantras, with pure water and flowers, [performs] the bath with the bathing mantra;
for the teacher who knows the Vedas and the Kula lineage, the knower of mantras should recite the mantra.
First, one should sprinkle water; second, likewise fragrance;
third, a flower; and fourth, incense and a lamp.
The fifth is the ritual of the mudrās, and the sixth is the placement of the mantras;
likewise, there is the placement on the limbs, the placement on the hands, and the six-limbed placement.
Having placed the goddess Sāvitrī, the Teacher becomes five-syllabled;
the knower of mantras [should do so] with the eight-syllable mantra of the Teacher and with the root mantra.
One should place the *mālāmantra*, the *kalāmantra*, and the *piṇḍamantra*;
likewise, the *Śrīrudra*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, and the Vedic chapters [should be recited] by the *kulālakas*.
The seventh offering should consist of sacrificial food (haviṣya), and the potter-women should be offered the oblation;
one should likewise worship the women at the door with the oblation and betel leaf.
Having likewise prepared the food offering for the guardian of the eastern gate, as well as for the Ṣaḍaṇa and Pratiṣaḍaṇa, the potter should perform the worship.
The potter is the food offering for the Teacher and his eight attendants;
the Gaṇarāja, however, should be placed first, in close proximity to the abode of the Teacher.
At the time of the offering, the potter should worship the eight-fold food offering (*naivedya*).
Thus, in the *Śāstāgama*, the procedure for daily worship is completed.
The Teacher is the foundation.
Next, the ritual procedure for the consecration of the Teacher is described.
He established that site as a place of installation for the removal of all sins, the bestowing of the fruits of all merit,

the warding off of all suffering, the bringing of all peace, the granting of all accomplishments, the destruction of all enemies, the eradication of all calamities, and the conferring of victory upon the king and his kingdom.

Having established the foundation for the abundance of wealth and grain, the increase of progeny, and the fruitfulness of crops for the sake of happiness, the Teacher, having determined the proper time, commenced [the work] during the northern course of the sun, in an auspicious month and under an auspicious lunar mansion,
when Jupiter was neither retrograde nor eclipsed, and Mars was not afflicted.
Having avoided the signs of Sagittarius, Aquarius, and Virgo, during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when Jupiter and Venus are rising and one is free from all defects,
the installation of all types of images is said to be performed under the auspicious lunar mansions.
Having prescribed the asterisms of Rohiṇī (Prājāpatya), Mūla, Puṣya, and Anurādhā; Soma, Āditya, and the Vasus;
Hasta, Śravaṇa, Citrā, Svāti, Pūṣan, and the Aśvins; and especially the Uttara-nakṣatras—of which Svāti is the most excellent.
One should arrange the days of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, joined with the seventh, fifth, third, eleventh, Bhadrā, and thirteenth lunar days.

Having determined the Libra ascendant as prescribed for the consort of Gemini, and having specifically determined the fixed signs, the lunar day, the asterism, and the zodiacal sign of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury—avoiding all defects such as those of aspect and so forth—one should have the rite of installation performed at the time thus described. That installation should be performed in four ways: the secret (rahasya) and the supreme-secret (paramaguhyaka).

One should perform the traditional ritual procedure: having prepared fresh sprouts and a mirror, one should carry out the rites up to the end of the *ratnanyāsa*, eye-opening (*nayanonmīlana*), purification of the image (*beraśodhana*), circumambulation of the village (*grāmapradakṣiṇa*), immersion in water (*jalādhivāsana*), consecration (*adhivāsana*), and the fire-oblation (*homakarma*);
during that time, one should recite the mantra with its limbs and sub-limbs (*sāṅgopāṅga*) and perform the ritual in this manner.
Having performed the rite for Varāha, one should thereafter recite the ritual procedure on a mountain,
in an inner sanctuary, on the side of a mountain, in a forest, in a cremation ground, in a wilderness, at a great tree, by a lake, in the corners of a well,
on the shore of the ocean, in a calamitous region, or in any such place where the installation is to take place.
Having performed the supreme procedure for installation in due order, the preceptor, having constructed a pavilion for the child in a determined location, should worship his own hand in its vicinity;
then, having caused the sounds of songs, dances, musical instruments, and the like to resound, and having especially worshipped the lineage of preceptors.

Through the lineage of the guru and disciple, one should perform hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption; the worship of the mantra, the practitioner, the deity, and the self; and the offerings ending with fish, honey, meat, blood, oblations, and fire-sacrifices, all while maintaining strict secrecy.

Having performed [the preliminary rites] according to the words of the tradition, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*)— including the ritual of the deposition of jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) and other such acts— by means of the secret procedural method, in a village, city, mountain, capital, market town (*kheṭaka*), or hamlet (*kharvaṭa*).
One should perform the consecration in due order.
O Bhūta, O Bhūta, I shall proclaim the characteristics of consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
which is meritorious, removes all sins, and wards off all suffering.
It is the supreme performer of all pacification, the ultimate bringer of all accomplishments,
the destroyer of all enemies, and the eradicator of all misfortunes.
It bestows victory and prosperity, brings happiness to kings and kingdoms,
and should be performed during the northern course of the sun, in an auspicious month, at a favorable moment.

O fool, at an auspicious and appropriate time, one should avoid Jupiter and Venus when they are eclipsed or retrograde; furthermore, one should avoid the signs of Scorpio, Sagittarius, Aquarius, and Virgo.
It should be performed in other months, avoiding the month of Doṣa;
specifically under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Uttarā-phalgunī, Mūla, Puṣya, and Anurādhā.
On a Monday, as well as under the asterisms of Vasu (Anurādhā), Hasta, and Śravaṇa;
and specifically under the Svāti asterism in the month of Caitra, or under Puṣya and Aśvinī.
On the days associated with Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, as well as with those [planets] themselves,
one should likewise observe the seventh, fifth, third, and eleventh lunar days.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada, as well as during the zodiac signs of Libra and Gemini,
a woman remains stable there, especially when it is a fixed sign.
The aspects and conjunctions of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury are always auspicious;
however, one should avoid the defect of aspect when the asterism or zodiac sign is "blind" (andha).
In those rites, the wise one who knows the ritual procedures should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
along with the supreme secret and the fourfold tradition (sampradāya) for a most trusted disciple.
The planting of fresh sprouts and the deposition of jewels are its fruit; and immediately following the opening of the eyes, the purification of the image occurs in due order.
One should perform the preliminary consecration with fresh water, or otherwise [with water from] a reservoir;
likewise, one should perform the fire-offering (homa) ritual, and at that time, the ceremonial bathing (snapana) should take place.
Thus the secret has been fully declared; now hear the supreme mystery:
on a mountain, or within a mountain cave, one should cause [the disciple] to move from side to side.
One may cause [the deity] to enter a forest, or even a cremation ground, or especially a reservoir;
or into a great tree, a pond, a well, or even a storehouse.
One should continuously worship [the deity] in sequence, whether at the ocean or in the forest;
and in each respective place, the installation and the supreme consecration should be performed in due order.
The supreme [method] is declared to be installation; now hear about secret installation.
Once the location has been determined by the preceptor, he should cause the installation of the child to be performed.
One should worship the manifested form (hastita) and perform singing, instrumental music, and the like;
or, for the sake of declaring the presence (sannidhi), one should effect its concealment—listen now to that presence.
Thus the secret procedure has been declared; now hear the tradition from that point on.
Having performed the placement of the *prapada* according to the rule, the wise one should cause it to be done.
Whether in a village, a city, a town, or a capital, or in a fortress,
on a mountain, or in an inferior location, one should install [the image] according to the prescribed ritual.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, in the case of a temple fire, a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*),
or a water-shed (*prapā*) should be constructed there, exactly as prescribed in the scriptures.
It was provided with sixteen pillars, measuring nine cubits [in height],
strewn with garlands of *darbha* grass, and beautifully adorned with flower garlands.
Having first performed the rite for auspiciousness and the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
one should likewise cause the sprouts to be offered on the sixteenth or the twelfth day.
One should cause the germination ceremony (aṅkura) to be performed on the ninth day, or even the seventh, or on the fifth day, or the third, or even on a single day.
An image is said to be of four kinds: made of metal, stone, clay, and wood; however, the clay image is traditionally considered to be of two types.
Those made of metal are to be known as threefold; those made of stone are slightly inferior;
those made of wood are considered middling; and likewise, those made of clay are the lowest.
Having become a bee, he should remain right there, joined with only his own measure;
he should cause a dwelling made of iron, stone, or wood to be constructed in that very place.
One should likewise have an image made of clay or of darbha grass;
one must carefully avoid one that is cracked, broken, or hollow.
A wise person, during the consecration of a Cakrabhāsa, should avoid the placement of jewels, the placement of water, strenuous effort, and the act of lying down.
O Lord, one should show the mirror and perform the rites of installation and so forth;
O Four-faced One, listen now to the characteristics of the preceptor.
Born of a noble family, having attained the lineage through the succession of gurus,
he is a teacher who has received initiation and consecration and is a protector of the conduct of the observance (samaya).
Constantly devoted to pleasing the Teacher, truthful in speech, with senses subdued,
possessing peaceful thoughts and endowed with patience, he avoids cruel deeds.
The Teacher has defined the characteristic of a master potter as being endowed with the proper conduct of a potter;
one who possesses such characteristics is called a master potter.
First is the placement of the jewels, second is the opening of the eyes,
third is the purification of the image, and fourth is the circumambulation of the village.

The fifth is the consecration with water (jalādhivāsa), and the sixth is the preparation of the bed (śayana). The seventh is the placement of the jars (kumbhavinyāsa), and the eighth is the rite of fire-oblation (homa-karma).
The ninth [rite] shall be the consecration (abhiṣeka), and the tenth is the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
In the center of that pavilion, however, there is a square enclosure wall (kuḍi).
Having determined the dimensions for the altars (vedikās), they should be four cubits wide and very extensive;
or likewise three cubits, or especially two cubits.
Having raised it by one cubit, with three feet and the hands bound together,
it should be level at the top and resemble the surface of a mirror.
After smearing it with cow dung, one should apply white powder;
thus the characteristics of the altar (vedikā) have been declared—now hear the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
p.
45) A square in the eastern direction, a shape like a womb (yoni) in the southeast,
a half-moon in the south, and a triangle in the southwest.
In the west (Vāruṇī) there should be a circular pit; in the northwest (Vāyavya), however, one with six corners;
in the north (Saumya), there should be a lotus-shaped pit; and in the northeast (Aiśānya), an eight-cornered one.
One should fashion a seven-cornered figure between the directions of Indra and Īśāna; one should dig a pit in the ground measuring one cubit, and it should be that same measure in width.
It should be provided with three girdles, or two, or even one;
its width on the wings should be equal to four times the height, and its height should be measured by that same standard.
One should fashion the girdle, the surrounding rim, and the womb according to the opening,
with lengths, widths, and heights of six, four, and four finger-breadths respectively.
In the center of the navel-pit, according to the ritual procedure for that rite,
one should fashion a navel nine finger-breadths in length and likewise elevated by one finger-breadth.
One should carefully avoid the *yoni* of a *yonyakuṇḍa* and the *nābhi* of a lotus-shaped (*padma*) *kuṇḍa*; indeed, this applies to all *kuṇḍas*.
All the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), beginning with the yoni-shaped, arise from the four-cornered [pit];
having thus fashioned the pits, this is remembered as their defining characteristic.
One should perform the smearing, the drying, and the binding;
one may kindle either a single fire or cause five fires to be prepared.

Alternatively, one may perform the rite according to the prescribed rules for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), whether they are three fires— the southern, eastern, and northern— or a single fire in the east.
One should begin the fire-oblation (homa) at night in the east, north, west, or south;
having prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules, or else a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila) is prescribed.
One should cause three lines to be drawn, with their tips pointing east and north;
first, one should have the arrangement of jewels made within the womb-chamber.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should likewise have a pavilion constructed;
there, one should prepare a sacrificial mound and place it upon the foundation.
Having worshipped the central womb [of the mandala], eight jars are likewise worshipped;
then, prior to the fire-offering ritual (homa-karma), one hundred oblations are made with the mantra of the Teacher (Śāstṛ).
Then, having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, one should perform the rites up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
Having likewise worshipped the womb-place (*garbhasthāna*), one should install the support together with the stone slab (*ādhāra-saśilā*).
Within the womb, however, one should sequentially arrange seven parts each for the Brahma,
Deva, Mānuṣa, and Piśāca [elements].
Having established that [image] among men, the wise one shall likewise describe the deposition of jewels; listen also to that reality from me.
Having placed a ruby in the center, a sapphire in the eastern direction,
a coral in the southeast, and a topaz in the south;
Having placed lapis lazuli in the southwest, one should place the gem in the west;
having placed gomedaka in the northwest, one should place pearls in the north.
Having placed crystal in the northeast, the knower of mantras should place these in sequence:
in the center with the Brahma-mantra and [the others] with the Indra-mantra.
Likewise, one should place the mantra of Agni in the region of Agni; having placed the *astra* (weapon-mantra) to the south, one should place it upon the head in the southwest (*nairṛtya*).
One should place the Parjanya-mantra in the southwest, the Aghora-mantra in the northwest, and the Vāyu-mantra in the north;
the Soma-mantra should be in the north, and the Īśa-mantra in the northeast.
Having thus performed the placement of the mantra according to the instructions of the master potter,
the preceptor should then perform the placement of the womb (garbha-nyāsa) together with the artisans.
One should wear a turban and an upper garment, and bear a golden ring;
above that, one should sow the nine seed-syllables or the seed-mantra.
One should place the jewels of the potters and artisans along with [the other] gems. Having thus performed the placement of the jewels, now hear about the opening of the eyes.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound there and spread darbha grass around it;
having placed the image in the center, it should be covered with a concealed cloth.
Facing either the eastern or the northern direction,
having performed the ritual bath for purification and wearing a white cloth as an upper garment, he should offer oblations into the sacred fire.
Facing either the east or the north, seated upon a pleasing seat,
and clothed in new garments, he should [recite] that respective mantra for a moment while looking at the twice-born.
Likewise, having drawn the golden needle and the eye, one should place the mantra;
and having likewise drawn the nine gates, one should [place] the principal seed-syllable according to the mantra.
One should prepare a vessel made of gold, silver, or even copper;
it should be filled with honey, milk, and ghee, and likewise with leaves.
One should place the honey-net (madhunetra) with the mantra beginning with "madhu pakṣaka";
having placed the milk in the heart, one should place the ghee with the foot-mantra.
One should worship the artisan there with the lines of the craft of goldsmithing and jewelry-making, and for the potters, with their hands.
In that regard, the wise man should avoid artisans and cause a *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) ceremony to be performed;
there should likewise be milk, clarified butter, honey, food, a tortoise, and fire.
Likewise, show a calf of cows according to the mantra of the Gāyatrīs;
and having shown the Brāhmaṇas [the image], [show it] with the mantra "brahmajajñānam."
Having shown [the mandala] to the people, who are the supreme refuge of all the gods, the liberation of the eyes has thus been declared; now hear the first purification.
He gave the eight nectars, the five medicinal herbs, and a bowl of water with jewels;
he also gave a portion of the earth and the consecration water of Kuru and Dakṣa.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there, extending from the feet to the hair, together with all the mixed [substances], and then install the water-pot (kumbha) upon it in due order.
One should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day there and have the rite of fire-oblation (homa) performed;
