one should especially offer oblations to the Teacher with the root mantra.
One should perform the consecration there and employ the garland-mantra;
the purification of the image has thus been explained, and now hear about the ritual immersion in water.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with every kind of finery,
accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, and filled with song and dance.
Whether on a stage, in a palanquin, or even in a chariot, let [the image] proceed with devotion,
surrounded by five yak-tail whisks, a parasol, and banners.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should perform the preliminary consecration in water—
either on a riverbank, at a lake, or even in pure water.
Or, in water reaching up to the navel, one should place a pedestal there;
having placed an image upon its top, one should cause the hanging beard to grow long.
Having first placed new cloth, sandalwood, and flowers with their heads toward the east,
one should then place the Teacher upon them with the upper garment spread out, using the root mantra.
One should place seven lotuses with the heart-mantra, surrounded by the *māyā*.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Narmadā, the Sarasvatī,
the Sindhu, the Godāvarī, and the Śrīkāverī— these are the seven rivers.
One should install that sacred site (tīrtha) with the very water-pot and with that very mantra;
one should then surround it with a garland of darbha grass, a canopy, and banners.
One should illuminate a vessel placed in water with a lamp for a day and night;
or one may let it remain for three nights, two nights, or even a single night.
The potter should immediately perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa);
this is called the ritual immersion in water—now hear about the altar and the bed.
The best [quantity] is ten droṇas, while the [next] is nine droṇas of rice;
half of that should be provided with rice-grains, and half of that again should be sesamum.
(50) On the altar, the preceptor should draw the Lord of Brahmins in the regions of the sky in the form of a lotus, having eight petals and a pericarp.
Above that is the deer-skin, and likewise above that the tiger-skin;
then there is Muṇḍikā upon the hair, and above that is Raktamuṇḍikā.
One should have white garments, a *muṇḍikā* headband, and new clothes prepared;
there, one should perform the consecration upon the bed in the proper sequence.
One should perform the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and a ritual bath according to the mantra;
then, in the center of the altar, [one should prepare] the image with arms [measured] by barley grains.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth using the root mantra, the knower of mantras,
after causing the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, should bind the protective thread (*rakṣābandha*).
Above that, however, is the bed-platform; it should have the head toward the east, the face upward, with hanging tassels, a secure binding, and be covered with a new cloth.
Then, having performed the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) according to the procedure seen in the scriptures,
one should place Īśāna on the head and Tatpuruṣa on the face.
Having placed Aghora in the heart, one should assign Vāma to the secret organ;
one should place Sadyojāta on the feet, and then again assign the limbs.
Having placed the heart-mantra upon the heart, one should place the head-mantra upon the head;
having placed the crest-mantra upon the crest, one should place the armor-mantra between the breasts.
Having placed the *netra* mantra upon the eyes and the *astra* mantra upon the region of the hands,
one should perform the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*, beginning with the crown (*makuṭa*), in their proper sequence.
One should place [the syllables] beginning with "Śāstā" using the root mantra and the heart mantra;
one should then sequentially place them on the head using the mantra "praśāntāya."
One should perform the placement of the mantra of Durgā beginning with the Praṇava;
one should place the Mālā-mantra, the Kalā-mantra, and the Piṇḍa-mantra.
Having placed the syllable *a* on the crown of the head, the syllable *ā* on the forehead,
the syllable *i* in the right eye, and the syllable *ī* in the left eye;
The letter *u* is in the right nostril, and the letter *ū* is in the left nostril;
the letter *ṛ* is in the right ear, and the letter *ṝ* is in the left eye.
The letter *ḷ* is on the right arm, and the letter *ḷ* is on the left arm;
the letter *e* is on the upper lip, and the letter *ai* is on the lower lip.
One should place the syllable *o* on the upper teeth and the syllable *au* on the lower teeth;
having placed the syllable *aṃ* on the palate, one should place the syllable *aḥ* at the root of the tongue.
The *ka*-group [of consonants] is on the right hand, the *ca*-group on the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group is on the right foot, and the *ta*-group on the left foot.
The syllable *pa* on the right wing, the syllable *pha* on the left wing,
the syllable *ba* at the region of the navel, and the syllable *bha* at the heart.
The letter *ma* is in the region of the elephant [the trunk], the letter *ya* is in the region of the fluids;
the letter *ra* is in the region of the blood, and the letter *la* is in the region of the flesh.
One should place the syllable *va* in the region of the flesh, the syllable *śa* in the marrow;
one should place the syllable *ṣa* in the region of the bones and the syllable *sa* in the semen.
Having assigned the letter *ha* to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), one should assign the letter *la* to the seed-syllables;
having assigned the letter *kṣa* to the feet, one thus performs the five-syllable mantra in sequence.
Having deposited the seed-syllable in the *liṅga*, one should deposit the *haṃsa* mantra and others in the heart;
with the *pāda-mantra*, one should place [the element] Earth in the feet, and food in the navel.
The knower of mantras should worship the heart with the *pāpaka* mantra, the feet with the *māseya* mantra,
and the head with the *ghaṭa* mantra, as does the potter.
Having placed the rājasa [element] in the heart and the tāmasa in the region of the navel,
the wise practitioner should place the sāttvika with the meat-mantra.

One should place the *jāgram* mantra on the forehead; the short [mantra] at the heart; and likewise, one should place the *suṣupti* mantra at the navel. Thus one should perform the placement of the mantras.

The knower of mantras, having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the root-mantra at the base (mūlādhāra) and the heart-mantra for the Teacher, the master of the lineage (kulālaka) should perform the worship.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should likewise perform the *pūraka* (inhalation) worship;
then, having performed the *kumbhaka* (retention), one should subsequently arrange the *kuṃbhas*.
Having taken nine new jars that are free from blemishes,
as well as eight low jars and water-pots;
Having wrapped it with a pure thread, one should purify it with water alone;
the wise man should prepare the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Furthermore, one should place nine water-pots in the middle of the altar,
and likewise, one should place sixteen jars on both sides of the entrance.
One should fill [the vessel] with pure water and cast in a *kūrca* (a bundle of grass),
joined with mango sprouts and provided with sandalwood and *agaru*.
Combined with gold, gems, and so forth, and endowed with moonlight,
[the water] containing the five gems is for the middle [offering], while that in the east is indeed for the *pādya* (water for washing the feet).
Having sipped water, one should place water in the southeast, and likewise the *arghya* offering in the southwest;
milk in the southwestern direction, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in the west.
Having placed curd in the northwest and turmeric in the north,
the wise man should establish kuśa grass in the northeast.
One should begin with a jar wrapped in new cloth and covered;
the wise preceptor should then place that central jar.
Having placed [the vessels] on both sides of the pitcher, one should set down the *vardhanī* at the beginning of the Goddess’s [position];
one should worship Śāstṛ in the *vardhanī*, the pitcher, and the Goddess.
One should place the eight forms (mūrtis) all around in the eight directions,
provided with four archways and accompanied by the eight auspicious symbols (maṅgalas).
A full water-pot of Varuṇa, a pair of lotuses, a fly-whisk,
a conch, a mirror, and a lamp— these are the eight auspicious objects for the Goddess Śrī.
One should worship the forms of the eight auspicious symbols on the exterior of the altar;
first, that which is named the eastern archway is prescribed as Śrīkara.
One should fashion the southern archway named Vaṃśaśā,
and one should fashion the western archway named Vimala.
The northern archway is proclaimed as the "Accomplishment of the Sacrifice" (yajñasiddhi).
One should place the archway, the water-pot (kalaśa), and the altar (vedi) on the exterior.
Having worshipped Ārya, Śāstṛ, Kṛṣṇā, Senādhibhūtavallabha,
and Ekavīryatanuvīrya with eight jars, one should proceed.
Having first established [the deities] as far as Īśāna, the wise one should likewise worship the ten weapons on the two outer sides of that [mandala].
The potter should worship the golden lotus, the discus, the goad, the conch, the noose, the vajra, the sword, the trident, and the staff.
One should worship the twelve Ādityas in sequence at the pitcher and the pillars;
one should then install the deities and their retinues with their respective mantras.
Having specifically placed madhūka and moḍhi there,
one should likewise worship with fragrance, flowers, and so forth, using a fresh cloth.
The Brahmin is indeed the seed, while the potter is the one most skilled in action;
he should perform the invocation of the Teacher and all other deities.
Having thus resolved, one should thereafter commence the fire-oblation (homa);
specifically, in the center of the nine divisions of the surrounding altar.
One should construct those sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) endowed with the characteristics previously described;
likewise, one should perform the rite of oblation (homa) and consecrate the pavilion and other structures.
Having churned fire, or [obtained it] from a sun-crystal, or indeed from the house of a Vedic scholar—
one should likewise [place] the Heart [mantra] and Tripāda as two, and the Head as two.
He should be made with four horns, six eyes, seven tongues, and two nostrils;
he should have seven hands and be adorned with all ornaments.
One should worship the fires there and have the enclosing sticks (paridhis) placed there;
one should prepare the supporting fuel-sticks (ādhāra-samidhau), as well as the kūrca-grass bundle and the girdle (mekhalā) in that very place.
Having placed the *praṇītā* vessel in the north, one should set down the *prokṣaṇī* in the southwest;
likewise, one should place the *brahmakūrca* in the south.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mung beans, black gram,
barley, sesame, śāli rice, wheat, wild rice, roasted flour, white mustard, and *nāgapā*.
Having offered curd, milk, and ghee individually into the center of the sacrificial pit,
[one should offer] fuel-sticks of palāśa, pure arka, aśvattha, and likewise udumbara.
In the first enclosure, one should plant Plakṣa, Khadira, Bilva, and Śamī trees;
from Indra and Agni up to Īśāna, there should likewise be ghee, Śamī, and barley.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for Brahmā, the Teacher, using the six limbs and the root seed-syllable (mūlabīja),
either one hundred and eight times, or half of that, or half of that again.
Everything should be performed with effort, each material separately;
likewise, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
When that day had dawned, having bathed and being made by that potter,
he put on new garments and a new upper cloth.
Afterward, the wise one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and worship the image (*bera*) again and again with perfumes, flowers, and lamps, just as before.
Having propitiated the Kumbha, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rule;
having performed [the rites] with all the primary offerings as before, one should then carry out the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, with the seed-syllable ŚĀSTṚ, one should cause the image to enter the house,
accompanied by the sounding of all musical instruments such as the conch, the dundubhī drum, and the bherī drum.
It was accompanied by the resonance of the Vedas and joined by great devotees with hymns,
sūtras, and great mantras that proclaim all auspiciousness.
One should cause the placement [of the deities] to be performed there; one should install the foundation stone (ādhāra-śilā), and between those two, one should establish the Teacher, the Lord Brahmā.
Having established the great image, the knower of mantras, having caused it to be well-situated with the root mantra,
should perform the eightfold binding of the limbs.
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the rite of offering the sprouts of rice and other grains;
there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made and cause the consecration (abhiṣeka) to be performed.
Thereafter, one should invoke within that [liṅga] the Teacher, the supreme deity—
two-eyed, two-armed, youthful, and beautiful in every limb.
Though joined with manifold times and adorned with all ornaments, it is partless and changeless; yet even so, it becomes possessed of parts.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village with a composed mind,
he should go before the preceptor and instruct him regarding the placement of the cows and other matters.

Having performed the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) rite for the Brahmins with musical instruments sounding before them, and having determined the characteristics of the hour, one should act during a favorable moment (*muhūrta*) and an auspicious conjunction (*sulagnaka*).
One should know that the *lolaja* and the *śāstibera* follow in due order;
having placed the *śāstā* upon the bathing altar, one should worship him in every respect.
Having meditated thus, the potter—or rather, the knower of mantras—should again perform the consecration;
with the root mantra, he should consecrate [the vessel] with the water-pot in the center.
One should recite the *mālā-gāyatrī* mantra over the rosary in the east;
with the branch-mantra (*śākhā-mantra*) in the southeast, and with the protective mantra (*āstra-mantra*) in the south.
One should recite the Heart-mantra in the southwest, the Armor-mantra in the west,
the Eye-mantra in the northwest, and the Gāyatrī in the north.
Having established [the deity] in the northeast with the seed-mantra and water,
and having thus installed the Lord of Gods, he then offered the vāmanaṃdana.
There, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) together with a fruit upon the throat;
afterwards, one should offer betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
The consecration has thus been explained; now hear the mantra and the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa).
Having placed the heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the head-mantra on the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* mantra upon the crest-lock, the *kavaca* on the region of the breasts,
and having assigned the *netra* mantra to the eyes, one should place the *astra* mantra upon the gaze.
One should worship the five limbs at the head, face, heart, navel, and feet;
one should place the root mantra, the best of sages, and the great scripture within the heart.
One should understand the weapons and arrange them according to the primary sequence;
one should likewise perform the transposition of the *vidyā*, just as in the case of the arrangement of the Vedas.
One should place all the Vedāṅgas and other [scriptures] on both sides;
one should place the flesh of the ear on the forehead, and the heart on the head.
One should place all the treatises on logic (tarka-śāstra) on both sides; having placed Sanskrit in the heart, one should place Paiśācī on the back.
Having first performed the placement of the feet with the seven mantras on the two feet,
and having likewise performed the placement of the Vidyā, one should then commence the placement of the worlds (loka-nyāsa).
Likewise, he should place the world of Rudra upon the head, the world of Viṣṇu on the forehead,
the world of Brahmā on the mouth, and the world of Candra in the heart.
One should place the space element in the region of the belly and the earthly realm at the placement of the feet;
then, having again placed the fingers according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the ritual placement.
Having performed this placement of the worlds (lokanyāsa), one should begin the placement of the deities (devatānyāsa).
Having placed Brahmāṇī on the head, Parameśvarī on the mouth,
Candrajā on the two eyes, and Sarasvatī on the tongue;
and having placed Viṣṇu on the heart, one should remember Vahniman on the face.
The world-protectors (Lokapālas) are on the sides, and likewise the Vasus are at the back.
Indra having obtained the surface of the belly, and the remaining deities the two sides;
thus the Teacher [has taught] that one should assign all the deities to the body in due order.

Having duly performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Goddess, of Brahman with its six limbs, and of the letters in their proper sequence, one should place the essential reality, which is one's own seed-syllable, in the heart.
Having arranged it thus at the proper time, one should cause the Brahmins to recite a blessing (*svasti*);
or else, having had the Brahmins proclaim an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should then perform the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
The twice-born should adorn [the deity] with garments and ornaments pleasing to the sight;
he should smear [the image] entirely with fragrances and decorate it with flowers and garlands.
One should worship with flowers, perfumes, and so forth, and with incense and lamps as ornaments; thereafter, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), food, and then, in sequence, food with ghee.
O best of the twice-born, one should cause to be given cakes, pure food, betel-leaf,
edibles, drinks, and all other such articles.
Having thus propitiated [the deity], one should arrange the retinue;
having summoned each by their respective names, one should assign them to their respective places.
One should place Sumukhī and Sulagnī on both sides;
likewise Viśvāmbarī, Viśvavarṇā, and Viśvagandhī.
One should establish Viśvamālī, Viśvoṣṇī, and Viśvapāda;
one should cause Viśvatoya to enter along with Viśvadarpaṇa.
Having likewise established the eight powers as mental, one should heat them;
[place] the elephant in the southern part and the horse in the northern direction.
And in this manner, one should perform the internal rites and establish them as "mental" (mānasa). Furthermore, the gatekeepers should be fashioned in the sixfold and the sixteenfold [arrangements].
The six limbs are on the right side, and the counter-limbs (prati-ṣaḍaṅga) are on the flank;
Vikṛti and Viṣakī are at the sides of the door, between the two Śaktis.
The *aṅgī*, the *sphuliṅgī*, the upper and lower lintels (*paṭṭikā*),
the *karṇī*, and the *kālamoḍī* are the presiding deities of the door-leaf (*kavāṭa*).
Caṇḍa and Āgama are at the eastern gate, while Pālaka,
Viśvāṅgin, and Svarūpin are the door-keepers of the two Śaktis.
Caṇḍākṣa-rāja and Caṇḍā are the guardians of the southern gate;
Vimalī and Viśvapadmī are the two śaktis of the southern gate.
O Rudra, the devotees have been completely scorched; Caṅgiri and Caṇḍamālin are the gatekeepers of the northern gate, while the Śaktis are at the sides of the gate.
The potter should install the form of the Asuras as prescribed;
the wise man should install a peacock on the northern side of the pavilion.
Mantravīra, Mahāvīra, and likewise Astravīra;
Gaṇavīra, Gaṇāvīra, and Halavīra, in that order.
These heroes are proclaimed as the eight heroes;
having likewise prepared a lotus-seat, one should cause them to be seated upon it.
The internal enclosure has been described; now hear about the external enclosure.
First, the wise practitioner should establish Airāvata in the east.
One should establish the Gaṇa king at the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) in the outer area;
one should have Airāvata with a beautiful face placed there in front.
Likewise, Śaṅkhavarṇa is in the south-east; then Kuṃbhodhara is in the south;
Siṃhavaktra is in the south-west; and Kukṣivaktra is in the west.
In the northwest, one should arrange Kapilavaktra; in the north, Gomukhī;
and likewise in the northeast, one should prepare the offering for Viśvaseṇa.
For the offering to the obstructions, the potter should install Agni and Vighneśvara;
to the south, the deity Brahmā; and to the southwest, the King of the Nāgas.
In the west is Indradeva, and likewise Mohinī in the northwest;
in the north is Somarāja, and Kṣetrapālaka in the northeast.
The potter should first install them starting from the east up to the northeast; this is declared as the second enclosure. Now hear about the third enclosure.
One should establish the presence of the Lord of the Gaṇas in the eastern direction;
the seat in the east has been so described, and the master of the lineage should install it there.
One should likewise designate the place for Agni, as well as that for Pālāśālaya;
in the south, the deity Saundara, and in the north, Kālabhūtaka.
The potter should place those who rescue from calamities in the northeast;
the wise one should place them starting from the east up to the northeast.
The third enclosure has been described; now hear of the fourth enclosure:
it consists of elephants, horses, dogs, bulls, cocks, rams, and lions.
The potter should place eight [figures], including a tiger and a peacock; this is declared as the fourth enclosure. Now hear about the fifth enclosure.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda,
Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka are proclaimed [as the eight elephants].
The potter should first place [the image] extending as far as Īśāna;
it should be made of one hundred and eight *niṣkas* of white gold, O best of the twice-born.
O King, one should present to the preceptor various kinds of wonderful things, various jewels and the like, as well as various cows and lands.
However, by means of that house-design which bestows all desired fruits,
with a beautiful floor and a water-pot for the gods, one shall find happiness therein.
It causes the destruction of all enemies and increases sons and grandsons;
indeed, that country shall experience abundance, and the king shall be victorious.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
one seeking a kingdom shall attain a kingdom, and one shall reach every desired land.
Having established the maṇḍala within the maṇḍala, one shall obtain every goal;
therefore, with all effort, the twice-born should appoint a teacher.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for consecration (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*) in the *Kulālaśāntitantra*.
May there be auspiciousness.
Having bathed and performed the ritual purification, Śrī-Ṛtu should install Vāgīśvarī.
One should place the *hṛdaya* [mantra] there; this is remembered as the rite of *garbhādhāna*. Having worshipped the head and the beginning of the mantra, one should perform the *puṃsavana*.
One should consecrate the *īśāna* [mantra] there and likewise perform the *sīmanta*.
One should have the *bali* offering performed for Viṣṇu with the *Puruṣa* mantra;
one should have the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*) performed with the *Vāmadeva* mantra.
For one newly born, the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*) is performed again with a mantra;
likewise, having offered oblations into the mouth with mantras, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) is performed.
One should offer oblations with the Śiromantra and perform the Cola rite;
one should cause the initiation (upanayana) to be performed with the Hṛdayamantra alone.
One should observe the Śukriya vow following the oblation of the Śikhā-mantra;
then, having offered the Vāmadeva oblation, one should perform the Samāvartana ceremony.
Having performed the marriage specifically with the mantra "praśāntāya," one who is skilled in the sacrificial offerings [should offer] oblations to the goddess Svāhā and Bhārī.

One should worship there with fire and perform the enclosures there. O Lord of the Mountain, neither caste, nor initiation, nor place and time, nor thirst, nor the fortnights, nor even the wish-fulfilling cow [is a hindrance] for every living being.
Just as one would act toward a teacher standing before them, so too should his son or grandson, or anyone initiated by him, act; in that regard, the preceptor should draw the form [of the deity].
That which is the supreme preliminary form of actions, others say is its opposite;
for the agent, as the sustainer, shall undergo death, which is the preliminary form of subsequent actions.
The syllable *pra* with the prefix *ut* is said to be the form *ḍambha*; *atikāra* is called *sṛṣṭi*.
The syllable *ṣṭha* with the vowel *ai* is endowed with form and is proclaimed as *pratiṣṭhā*.
This is the procedure for worship (*arcanavidhi*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the worship of the Teacher; listen to the sequence of rites for the worship of the Great Teacher and the other deities.
Brahmā said: [I approach] the God of gods, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa,
the Lord of beings, the Sovereign of the worlds, O Destroyer of sins, O Lord of the universe!
The Teacher [spoke of] the various types of images and the sequence of the ritual for the worship of the potter,
having offered three handfuls of flowers with palms joined and placing them upon his head.
Īśvara said:
O Lotus-Seated One, listen to the classification of images for the worship of the Teacher.
The Teacher is the most excellent performer of worship; he is the potter initiated into the scriptures.
It removes all sins, and its worship should indeed be performed day after day.
65) The Ritual of Ashes:
The ritual manual, the human ritual manual, and likewise the non-ritual manual.
The ash itself is said to be threefold; listen now, O Skanda, to that very [classification].

One should cause [the rite] to be performed for a cow, a barren woman, a maiden, and bulls; however, in the case of a woman who has recently given birth, one should perform it with clarified butter for ten days, increasing by a hundred [oblations] in sequence.
Having taken cow dung and a lump [of earth] with the root mantra,
one should burn them with the Śiva-fire and prepare that ash according to the ritual procedure.
One should burn the four powders with goat's milk, along with the lump itself, in the sacrificial fire; this ash is here described as the secondary alternative (anukalpa).
With the body of the forest-dweller (vanākadeha), there is ash and the earth that holds bliss;
through the cessation of the five lamps and so forth, Sarasvatī alone remains.
The measure above is merely a measure, while the middle measure and so forth constitute the metrical unit.
The Teacher’s root mantra shall consist of one foot and three measures; the Guide shall arise from the eyes.
Oṃ Hrīṃ! Salutation to the son of Hara, the destroyer of enemies, the bestower of sons, whose vehicle is an elephant, the great wielder of weapons.

I bow to the lotus feet of Vighneśvara, the elephant-faced one, who is served by hosts of spirits, who feeds on the essence of the kapittha and jambū fruits, the son of Umā, and the cause of the destruction of sorrow.

I bow to Gaṇanātha in his true form, saffron-colored, endowed with four arms, possessing the face of an elephant, holding a goad and a basket, bearing a goad and a noose, and having sweets for teeth and a beautiful noose.

The elephant-faced Siddha, with a single tusk on the right, three eyes, many faces, and the form of all beings; ancient, the best of immortals, worthy of supreme worship, red in color, and the Lord of Auspiciousness.
I bow to the son of Paśupati, the Lord, the King of Obstacles.

"Salutation to Vighneśvara"—this is the invocation (*āvāhana*). "Salutation to Gaṇādhyakṣa; salutation to Phālacandra; salutation to Gajānana. [I perform] the bathing (*snāpana*), the confinement (*sannirodhana*), the striking (*tāḍana*), the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*), and I prepare the water for the feet (*pādya*), the sipping water (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the bath (*snāna*).

Having offered perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, garments, sacred threads, and ornaments for the sake of decoration, as well as these unbroken grains (*akṣata*), a coconut offering, plantain fruit, jaggery, betel leaf, and food oblation (*naivedya*), and having made a formal request according to the ritual procedure, one should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for Vighneśvara.

(p. 67) Within this great flood of water, which is sustained by the inconceivable and immeasurable power of this glorious Great Blessed One, the Great Person, the glorious Viṣṇu, the primordial Nārāyaṇa, there wander many...

Within this great fragment of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-khaṇḍa), which is surrounded by earth, water, fire, air, ether, the Great Principle (mahat), and the Unmanifest (avyakta), and consisting of ten million such fragments— in the midst of this, upon the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), the Tortoise (kūrma), Ananta, and the eight elephants of the quarters, are situated the worlds of Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Nitala, Rasātala, Talātala, and Mahātala.

Above the regions known as Pātāla, and below the worlds of Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka, [the world] is adorned by the circle of a thousand hoods of Śeṣa, the king of serpents, who acts as a great pillar; it is supported by the trunks of the elephants of the quarters and encircled by the Lokāloka mountain.

Surrounded by oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and pure water, in the midst of the islands of Jambū, Plakṣa, Śāka, Śālmali, and Puṣkara— resembling Indra, Kaśeru, Tāmra-varṇa, Gabhastimat, Nāga, Saumya, Gandharva, Cāraṇa, and Mahā-saroruha— there are fifty [continents].

For the purpose of immediately dispelling the sins accumulated through the activities of the mind, speech, body, and the organs of action upon the terrestrial sphere extending for ten million yojanas.
By the command of Śiva-Śambhu, in the second *parārdha* of the current Brahmā,
during the illustrious Śveta-varāha-kalpa, in the Vaivasvata-manvantara, on the surface of the lunar fortnight, in the twenty-eighth Yuga,
in the first quarter of the Kali-yuga, in Jambūdvīpa, in Bhāratavarṣa, in the Bharata-khaṇḍa, on the southern side of Mount Meru.

For the purpose of destroying sins, for the purpose of exhausting evil deeds, for the purpose of pacifying all misfortunes, for the purpose of attaining the fourfold goals of human life— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— for the purpose of obtaining all auspiciousness, and for the purpose of expiation for the three types of actions (mental, vocal, and physical) committed through the three organs (mind, speech, and body).
In the presence of the Sun, in the presence of the Aśvattha tree (p. 69), in the presence of a deity or a Brahmin, in the presence of Īśvara, and in the presence of Viṣṇu.

In the presence of the Great Teacher Sadāśiva, for the sake of the purification of the pavilion, the purification of the site, the purification of the vessels, the purification of myself, and the purification of the materials, I shall perform the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) on behalf of the Great Teacher named Aśarman of the Śiva lineage.
Hari Om!
May there be long life; may there be abundance of wealth and grain; may there be an increase in sons and grandsons; may there be well-being; may all be auspicious.

May there be good fortune! Oṃ, may there be prosperity and accomplishment! Oṃ, may there be fulfillment of desires! Oṃ, may there be peace; may there be auspiciousness! Oṃ, may there be longevity; may there be health! Oṃ, for the sacrifice of the son Indra—may there be the splendor of the earth, the brilliance of the sun, and the power of the wind; may there be victory through Viṣṇu!
Having partaken of the meal, [he recites] the Veda-anga: "Oṃ, may there be prosperity immediately; may the god Indra bestow glory and the lotus-flower.
O Śatakratu, grant increase to the son of Indra and long life.
[May there be] the Aśvattha tree, the gift of a vessel of sesame, pure water, and the satiation of Brahmins. [The study of] the Vedas..."

O Teacher, together with the assembly of sages, [you have come] to this holy field situated between Mount Meru and Mount Kailāsa on the peak of Manu, amidst these oceans such as the Gaṅgā and others, which are like life itself to living beings at your sacred ford.

From the leading forth [of the image], twelve [verses] less eight [are recited]: "May the auspicious day dwell here," and so forth; "O Aja, may there be well-being for your lordship. *Oṃ*, "O Potter," [this is] the auspicious day. *Oṃ*, "O God Aghora," [this is] the auspicious day.
That which was previously remembered as the presence of the deities is indeed the first step. *Oṃ*, "May the eleven Rudras be pleased. *Oṃ*.

May the twelve Ādityas be pleased. May the eight Vasus, Prajāpati, and Indra be pleased. May Subrahmaṇya and Soma-rāja be pleased. May the single-tusked Gaṇapati, the elephant-faced Vināyakas, Ārya Śāstṛ, Kṛṣṇa, Senāpati, Bhūtanātha, Bhūtavallabha, and Yogabhairava be pleased.
May the eight archer-heroes be pleased! May Airāvata, Vighneśvara, Brahmā, Nāgarāja, Mohinī, Devendra, Soma, and the Kṣetrapālas be pleased! May the world-protectors be pleased;
may the eight heroes be pleased; may the eight Śaktis be pleased; may the eight auspicious symbols be pleased!

May the Four Great Kings be pleased. May the Seven Sages be pleased. May the Noble Blessed Lady, Bhāryā, Kālī, Nārī, Mṛgavājinī, and the Goddess Durgā be pleased. There is the Banner-bearer; may Aśvavāhana, Vajrāyudha, Viśvarūpa, and Madhukara be pleased. May the Great Teacher be pleased.

May the Mother of the World, the Knower of Dharma, seated upon a lotus, be pleased for the sake of prosperity; may the eight guardians of the world be pleased; may Agni, the god, the bearer of oblations, the consumer of offerings, who is beneficial in every way, be pleased; and may the Lord of Knowledge, the Wielder of the Discus, be pleased for the attainment of the intended purpose.

May the sixty-four arts, the Mother of the Gods, Vidyeśvara, and Nārāyaṇa—may these thirteen be pleased. May all the lunar mansions be pleased; may there be abundance of all wealth and grain. Oṃ, peace, peace, peace! Hariḥ Oṃ.
May there be auspiciousness! Homage to the gurus!
The seasons— spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season—
six; the months— Caitra, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada,
Āśvina, Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, Māgha, and Phālguna— twelve.
The days [of the week]: Āditya is Bhānu; Soma is Indu; Maṅgala is Bhauma; Budha is Saumya; Bṛhaspati is Guru; Śukra is Bhṛgu; Śani is Manda.
The seven seers.
In the east, Pulastya [installed] the sequence of the gods' fire and soma-essence;
in the south he established Nārada, and in the southwest, Bhṛgu.
Vasiṣṭha [placed] Mārkaṇḍeya in the western quarter (vāruṇa) and [the others] from Vāyu in due order; having placed Kauśika in the lunar (saumya) quarter, he likewise placed Agastya and Īśa.
